newsitem.title: USA: U.S. oat output seen at risk of declining further.
newsitem.headline: U.S. oat output seen at risk of declining further.

text.p: The possibility of planting delays in the northern U.S. Plains and the relative attractiveness of competing cash crops could further shrink U.S. oat acreage and output in 1997, grain experts said.

Pat Henderson, executive director of the American Oat Association in Minneapolis, said that unless the northern Plains see a gradual warming trend over the next two months, severe flooding could occur as the heavy snow pack melts, causing planting delays for oats and other spring crops.
"There's quite the concern for flooding if we don't get a gradual decrease in this amount of snow," Henderson said.

Oats would likely be hit hardest by spring planting delays because they are usually the earliest planted of the spring crops. Unlike spring wheat, for example, oats are planted early because they make optimal use of cool weather during spring and early summer.
Henderson said planting delays over the past two years had caused growers to switch to other crops, thereby shrinking the available oat acreage.
"They usually try to get oats in by April, but of course the last few years we've had (delays due to) such horrendous weather situations," she said.
In its most recent crop report, the North Dakota Agricultural Statistics Service said the average snow depth for the state was 17.9 inches on Feb 2, compared to 10.4 inches a year earlier.

Duane Berglund, professor and extension agronomist at North Dakota State University in Fargo, N.D., said that apart from planting delays, oat acreage could also be threatened as producers switch to more competitive cash crops.
"There's so much interest in some of the other crops like peas, canola and dry beans, that oats are almost getting to be like a minor crop," Berglund said.
"I think in time, oats will almost be a contract crop. I think it's coming to that," he said.

USDA's January 10 annual crop production report showed a decline in U.S. oats production over the past two years. U.S. growers produced 155.2 million bushels of oats in 1996, down from 162.0 million in 1995 and 229.0 million in 1994.
In September, USDA said planted U.S. oats acreage declined to 4.66 million acres in 1996, down from 6.37 million acres in 1995 and 6.64 million in 1994.
In North Dakota, typically the largest U.S. oats producer, harvested acres in 1996 were 380,000 bushels, down from 450,000 in 1995 and 550,000 acres in 1994.
